questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Literary Genres: Prose, Drama, and Poetry
questions.Question: Which of the following is the fundamental distinguishing feature of Drama compared to Prose and Poetry?
questions.OptionA: It is written predominantly in dialogue and actions designed to be performed on a stage before an audience
questions.OptionB: It is arranged strictly in rhythmic metered stanzas with a uniform rhyme scheme
questions.OptionC: It is narrated entirely through past-tense descriptive prose paragraphs by an omniscient voice
questions.OptionD: It avoids characterization and focuses exclusively on landscape description
questions.Option_a: It is written predominantly in dialogue and actions designed to be performed on a stage before an audience
questions.Option_b: It is arranged strictly in rhythmic metered stanzas with a uniform rhyme scheme
questions.Option_c: It is narrated entirely through past-tense descriptive prose paragraphs by an omniscient voice
questions.Option_d: It avoids characterization and focuses exclusively on landscape description
questions.Explanation: Drama is unique among the three major genres because its primary medium is dialogue and stagecraft intended for live theatrical representation.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Literary Genres: Prose, Drama, and Poetry
questions.Question: A novel that traces the psychological, moral, and social development of a protagonist from youth to maturity is known as a:
questions.OptionA: Picaresque novel
questions.OptionB: Bildungsroman (coming-of-age novel)
questions.OptionC: Epistolary novel
questions.OptionD: Gothic romance
questions.Option_a: Picaresque novel
questions.Option_b: Bildungsroman (coming-of-age novel)
questions.Option_c: Epistolary novel
questions.Option_d: Gothic romance
questions.Explanation: A Bildungsroman (German for 'formation novel') focuses on the psychological growth and moral education of the main character from childhood into adulthood.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Literary Genres: Prose, Drama, and Poetry
questions.Question: A dramatic composition that employs highly exaggerated characters, absurd physical humour, and improbable situations to evoke boisterous laughter is classified as a:
questions.OptionA: Morality play
questions.OptionB: Tragic flaw
questions.OptionC: Farce
questions.OptionD: Heroic tragedy
questions.Option_a: Morality play
questions.Option_b: Tragic flaw
questions.Option_c: Farce
questions.Option_d: Heroic tragedy
questions.Explanation: Farce is a sub-genre of low comedy characterized by ridiculous plots, horseplay, visual gags, and deliberate absurdities designed purely for amusement.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Literary Genres: Prose, Drama, and Poetry
questions.Question: What is an 'Epistolary Novel'?
questions.OptionA: A factual government report published in gazette chapters
questions.OptionB: A narrative told exclusively in heroic rhyming verse couplets
questions.OptionC: A story depicting adventures of rogue bandits traveling on high-seas pirate ships
questions.OptionD: A novel narrated entirely or largely through an exchange of written letters or journal entries
questions.Option_a: A factual government report published in gazette chapters
questions.Option_b: A narrative told exclusively in heroic rhyming verse couplets
questions.Option_c: A story depicting adventures of rogue bandits traveling on high-seas pirate ships
questions.Option_d: A novel narrated entirely or largely through an exchange of written letters or journal entries
questions.Explanation: An epistolary novel develops its plot and character perspectives through correspondence (letters, diary entries, or documents) written by characters.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Literary Genres: Prose, Drama, and Poetry
questions.Question: A theatrical play written specifically to be read in private by a reader rather than performed before an audience on a public stage is a:
questions.OptionA: Closet drama
questions.OptionB: Melodrama
questions.OptionC: Pantomime
questions.OptionD: Miracle play
questions.Option_a: Closet drama
questions.Option_b: Melodrama
questions.Option_c: Pantomime
questions.Option_d: Miracle play
questions.Explanation: A closet drama is a drama intended by the playwright to be read privately or recited in a small group rather than staged in a physical theatre.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Literary Genres: Prose, Drama, and Poetry
questions.Question: Which sub-genre of poetry is characterized by a formal, sustained lyric lament mourning the death of an individual or tragic event?
questions.OptionA: Ballad
questions.OptionB: Elegy
questions.OptionC: Panegyric
questions.OptionD: Epic
questions.Option_a: Ballad
questions.Option_b: Elegy
questions.Option_c: Panegyric
questions.Option_d: Epic
questions.Explanation: An elegy is a dignified, melancholic lyric poem mourning the loss of a deceased loved one or reflecting somberly on mortality.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Literary Genres: Prose, Drama, and Poetry
questions.Question: A long narrative poem composed on an elevated style celebrating the heroic exploits of legendary characters or founding national deeds is a(n):
questions.OptionA: Limerick
questions.OptionB: Ode
questions.OptionC: Epic
questions.OptionD: Villanelle
questions.Option_a: Limerick
questions.Option_b: Ode
questions.Option_c: Epic
questions.Option_d: Villanelle
questions.Explanation: An epic is an extended narrative poem written in grand poetic diction dealing with heroic or mythological deeds central to a culture's identity (e.g., Homer's Iliad, Sundiata).

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Literary Genres: Prose, Drama, and Poetry
questions.Question: In dramatic literature, the spoken words of an actor directed privately to the audience, which by theatrical convention are inaudible to other characters onstage, constitute a(n):
questions.OptionA: Prologue
questions.OptionB: Soliloquy
questions.OptionC: Dialogue
questions.OptionD: Aside
questions.Option_a: Prologue
questions.Option_b: Soliloquy
questions.Option_c: Dialogue
questions.Option_d: Aside
questions.Explanation: An aside is a brief remark addressed to the audience (or another selected character) that other characters on stage are presumed not to hear.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Literary Genres: Prose, Drama, and Poetry
questions.Question: How does a 'Soliloquy' differ essentially from a 'Monologue' in drama?
questions.OptionA: A soliloquy is delivered when the character is alone on stage disclosing private inner thoughts, whereas a monologue is an extended speech addressed to other characters
questions.OptionB: A soliloquy must always be sung to orchestral music, while a monologue is whispered off-stage
questions.OptionC: A monologue can only be delivered by the tragic chorus, whereas a soliloquy is spoken by minor clownish characters
questions.OptionD: A soliloquy occurs exclusively in the final scene of Act Five, while a monologue opens Act One
questions.Option_a: A soliloquy is delivered when the character is alone on stage disclosing private inner thoughts, whereas a monologue is an extended speech addressed to other characters
questions.Option_b: A soliloquy must always be sung to orchestral music, while a monologue is whispered off-stage
questions.Option_c: A monologue can only be delivered by the tragic chorus, whereas a soliloquy is spoken by minor clownish characters
questions.Option_d: A soliloquy occurs exclusively in the final scene of Act Five, while a monologue opens Act One
questions.Explanation: A soliloquy reveals the speaker's internal psychological state while alone on stage, while a monologue is an uninterrupted speech delivered in the presence of other characters.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Literary Genres: Prose, Drama, and Poetry
questions.Question: A dramatic genre characterized by exaggerated emotional conflicts, sensational thrills, and stereotyped virtuous heroes versus unredeemable villains is:
questions.OptionA: High comedy
questions.OptionB: Melodrama
questions.OptionC: Comedy of manners
questions.OptionD: Pastoral masque
questions.Option_a: High comedy
questions.Option_b: Melodrama
questions.Option_c: Comedy of manners
questions.Option_d: Pastoral masque
questions.Explanation: Melodrama emphasizes sensationalism, heightened emotionalism, simplistic moral polarities (pure good vs absolute evil), and often happy endings over deep characterization.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Literary Genres: Prose, Drama, and Poetry
questions.Question: A work of literature that uses irony, ridicule, and wit to expose and criticize human folly, institutional corruption, or vice with the aim of provoking reform is a:
questions.OptionA: Tragic catharsis
questions.OptionB: Eulogy
questions.OptionC: Satire
questions.OptionD: Hagiography
questions.Option_a: Tragic catharsis
questions.Option_b: Eulogy
questions.Option_c: Satire
questions.Option_d: Hagiography
questions.Explanation: Satire employs humor, irony, and sarcasm to expose societal or individual vices, abuses, and foolishness to stimulate corrective moral improvement.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Literary Genres: Prose, Drama, and Poetry
questions.Question: A poem addressed formally and enthusiastically to a person, an abstract quality, or a physical entity, typically written in an elevated, celebratory lyric style, is a(n):
questions.OptionA: Hymn
questions.OptionB: Sonnet
questions.OptionC: Ballad
questions.OptionD: Ode
questions.Option_a: Hymn
questions.Option_b: Sonnet
questions.Option_c: Ballad
questions.Option_d: Ode
questions.Explanation: An ode is an elaborately structured, exalted lyric poem expressing dignified admiration or reverent meditation toward a specific subject.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Elements of Fiction: Plot, Setting, Theme, and Narrative Perspective
questions.Question: In narrative fiction, what is the crucial distinction between 'Story' and 'Plot' as famously formulated by E.M. Forster?
questions.OptionA: A story is a chronological narrative of events, while a plot emphasizes causality and why events happen
questions.OptionB: A story is always written in prose, whereas a plot must be written in blank verse
questions.OptionC: A plot refers only to non-fiction memoirs, while a story applies to fairy tales
questions.OptionD: A story describes minor characters, while a plot describes solely the tragic hero
questions.Option_a: A story is a chronological narrative of events, while a plot emphasizes causality and why events happen
questions.Option_b: A story is always written in prose, whereas a plot must be written in blank verse
questions.Option_c: A plot refers only to non-fiction memoirs, while a story applies to fairy tales
questions.Option_d: A story describes minor characters, while a plot describes solely the tragic hero
questions.Explanation: As Forster explained: 'The king died and then the queen died' is a story (chronology); 'The king died and then the queen died of grief' is a plot (causal relationship).

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Elements of Fiction: Plot, Setting, Theme, and Narrative Perspective
questions.Question: The moment of highest emotional tension, greatest dramatic intensity, or decisive turning point in a narrative plot is the:
questions.OptionA: Exposition
questions.OptionB: Climax
questions.OptionC: Inciting incident
questions.OptionD: Denouement
questions.Option_a: Exposition
questions.Option_b: Climax
questions.Option_c: Inciting incident
questions.Option_d: Denouement
questions.Explanation: The climax is the peak of narrative tension where the primary conflict reaches its decisive turning point.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Elements of Fiction: Plot, Setting, Theme, and Narrative Perspective
questions.Question: The final unravelling, clarification, or resolution of the intricate complications of a dramatic or narrative plot is called the:
questions.OptionA: Catharsis
questions.OptionB: Epilogue
questions.OptionC: Denouement
questions.OptionD: Foreshadowing
questions.Option_a: Catharsis
questions.Option_b: Epilogue
questions.Option_c: Denouement
questions.Option_d: Foreshadowing
questions.Explanation: Denouement (from the French for 'unknotting') is the final phase of plot following the falling action where mysteries are solved and conflicts concluded.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Elements of Fiction: Plot, Setting, Theme, and Narrative Perspective
questions.Question: A narrative technique whereby the story begins in the middle of crucial events rather than at the chronological starting point is known as:
questions.OptionA: Stream of consciousness
questions.OptionB: Deus ex machina
questions.OptionC: Flashforward
questions.OptionD: In medias res
questions.Option_a: Stream of consciousness
questions.Option_b: Deus ex machina
questions.Option_c: Flashforward
questions.Option_d: In medias res
questions.Explanation: 'In medias res' (Latin for 'into the midst of things') is the classical convention of opening a narrative at a critical midpoint of action, filling in background via flashbacks.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Elements of Fiction: Plot, Setting, Theme, and Narrative Perspective
questions.Question: A literary device that provides subtle hints, clues, or warnings about events that will happen later in the narrative is:
questions.OptionA: Foreshadowing
questions.OptionB: Backstory
questions.OptionC: Allusion
questions.OptionD: Irony
questions.Option_a: Foreshadowing
questions.Option_b: Backstory
questions.Option_c: Allusion
questions.Option_d: Irony
questions.Explanation: Foreshadowing prepares the reader emotionally and intellectually for impending developments by planting anticipatory clues.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Elements of Fiction: Plot, Setting, Theme, and Narrative Perspective
questions.Question: A character who contrasts sharply with another character (usually the protagonist) to highlight particular qualities or personality traits of the latter is a:
questions.OptionA: Antagonist
questions.OptionB: Foil
questions.OptionC: Caricature
questions.OptionD: Confidant
questions.Option_a: Antagonist
questions.Option_b: Foil
questions.Option_c: Caricature
questions.Option_d: Confidant
questions.Explanation: A foil is a character whose temperament, choices, or flaws contrast directly with another character, illuminating the latter's distinctive nature (e.g., Banquo to Macbeth).

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Elements of Fiction: Plot, Setting, Theme, and Narrative Perspective
questions.Question: Which narrative point of view features an all-knowing narrator who stands outside the action, observing the thoughts, feelings, and motives of all characters?
questions.OptionA: First-person participant
questions.OptionB: Third-person limited
questions.OptionC: Third-person omniscient
questions.OptionD: Second-person objective
questions.Option_a: First-person participant
questions.Option_b: Third-person limited
questions.Option_c: Third-person omniscient
questions.Option_d: Second-person objective
questions.Explanation: The third-person omniscient narrator possesses god-like insight into the interior minds, hidden motives, and simultaneous actions of all characters in the narrative.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Elements of Fiction: Plot, Setting, Theme, and Narrative Perspective
questions.Question: A first-person narrator whose credibility, perception, or honesty is compromised by youth, mental instability, bias, or moral corruption is a(n):
questions.OptionA: Dramatic narrator
questions.OptionB: Omniscient narrator
questions.OptionC: Factual observer
questions.OptionD: Unreliable narrator
questions.Option_a: Dramatic narrator
questions.Option_b: Omniscient narrator
questions.Option_c: Factual observer
questions.Option_d: Unreliable narrator
questions.Explanation: An unreliable narrator cannot be fully trusted by the reader to present an accurate, objective, or truthful account of story events.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Elements of Fiction: Plot, Setting, Theme, and Narrative Perspective
questions.Question: In fiction, a 'Round Character' as defined by E.M. Forster is one who:
questions.OptionA: Possesses psychological depth, complexity, and the capacity to surprise the reader convincingly through growth or change
questions.OptionB: Is constructed around a single immutable trait and never evolves throughout the novel
questions.OptionC: Appears only in a single brief scene to deliver comedic relief
questions.OptionD: Has no physical name and represents an abstract philosophical concept
questions.Option_a: Possesses psychological depth, complexity, and the capacity to surprise the reader convincingly through growth or change
questions.Option_b: Is constructed around a single immutable trait and never evolves throughout the novel
questions.Option_c: Appears only in a single brief scene to deliver comedic relief
questions.Option_d: Has no physical name and represents an abstract philosophical concept
questions.Explanation: Round characters are multi-dimensional, complex, and dynamic, capable of genuine psychological development, unlike flat (one-dimensional) characters.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Elements of Fiction: Plot, Setting, Theme, and Narrative Perspective
questions.Question: The central insight, fundamental underlying idea, or philosophical truth about human nature explored throughout a literary text is its:
questions.OptionA: Plot
questions.OptionB: Theme
questions.OptionC: Setting
questions.OptionD: Tone
questions.Option_a: Plot
questions.Option_b: Theme
questions.Option_c: Setting
questions.Option_d: Tone
questions.Explanation: Theme is the overarching, meaningful concept or commentary on life that a literary work communicates through its characters, conflicts, and events.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Elements of Fiction: Plot, Setting, Theme, and Narrative Perspective
questions.Question: A recurring image, object, phrase, or symbolic motif that reinforces the central theme of a literary work is a:
questions.OptionA: Epiphany
questions.OptionB: Paradox
questions.OptionC: Motif
questions.OptionD: Hyperbole
questions.Option_a: Epiphany
questions.Option_b: Paradox
questions.Option_c: Motif
questions.Option_d: Hyperbole
questions.Explanation: A motif is an identifiable repeating element (image, sound, word, or pattern) that helps develop and inform the central theme of a work.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Elements of Fiction: Plot, Setting, Theme, and Narrative Perspective
questions.Question: The historical period, geographical location, physical landscape, and social environment in which the action of a narrative occurs is the:
questions.OptionA: Genre
questions.OptionB: Atmosphere
questions.OptionC: Subplot
questions.OptionD: Setting
questions.Option_a: Genre
questions.Option_b: Atmosphere
questions.Option_c: Subplot
questions.Option_d: Setting
questions.Explanation: Setting encompasses the physical coordinates of time, place, historical epoch, and sociological milieu in which the fictional events unfold.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Figurative Language, Tropes, and Rhetorical Devices
questions.Question: What figure of speech is exemplified in the phrase: 'The classroom was a noisy bee hive of bustling activity'?
questions.OptionA: Metaphor
questions.OptionB: Simile
questions.OptionC: Hyperbole
questions.OptionD: Synecdoche
questions.Option_a: Metaphor
questions.Option_b: Simile
questions.Option_c: Hyperbole
questions.Option_d: Synecdoche
questions.Explanation: A metaphor asserts an implicit, direct comparison between two unlike things by equating one with the other without using 'like' or 'as'.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Figurative Language, Tropes, and Rhetorical Devices
questions.Question: Identify the figure of speech in: 'The old oak tree groaned in agony as the ferocious wind tore at its branches'.
questions.OptionA: Litotes
questions.OptionB: Personification
questions.OptionC: Metonymy
questions.OptionD: Euphemism
questions.Option_a: Litotes
questions.Option_b: Personification
questions.Option_c: Metonymy
questions.Option_d: Euphemism
questions.Explanation: Personification attributes human qualities, emotions, or physical actions (groaning in agony) to inanimate objects or nature.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Figurative Language, Tropes, and Rhetorical Devices
questions.Question: The rhetorical juxtaposition of two contradictory or incongruous words side by side, such as 'deafening silence' or 'sweet sorrow', is an:
questions.OptionA: Antithesis
questions.OptionB: Paradox
questions.OptionC: Oxymoron
questions.OptionD: Hyperbole
questions.Option_a: Antithesis
questions.Option_b: Paradox
questions.Option_c: Oxymoron
questions.Option_d: Hyperbole
questions.Explanation: An oxymoron is a compact figure of speech that pairs two contradictory terms together in immediate contact.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Figurative Language, Tropes, and Rhetorical Devices
questions.Question: A statement that appears self-contradictory or absurd on the surface, but reveals a deeper, profound underlying truth upon reflection, is a:
questions.OptionA: Solecism
questions.OptionB: Oxymoron
questions.OptionC: Malapropism
questions.OptionD: Paradox
questions.Option_a: Solecism
questions.Option_b: Oxymoron
questions.Option_c: Malapropism
questions.Option_d: Paradox
questions.Explanation: A paradox is an apparently contradictory proposition or statement that, when closely investigated, expresses a valid or insightful truth (e.g. 'The child is father of the man').

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Figurative Language, Tropes, and Rhetorical Devices
questions.Question: Which figure of speech substitutes the name of an attribute, adjunct, or closely associated thing for the thing actually meant (e.g., 'The pen is mightier than the sword')?
questions.OptionA: Metonymy
questions.OptionB: Synecdoche
questions.OptionC: Onomatopoeia
questions.OptionD: Apostrophe
questions.Option_a: Metonymy
questions.Option_b: Synecdoche
questions.Option_c: Onomatopoeia
questions.Option_d: Apostrophe
questions.Explanation: Metonymy substitutes an associated concept for the subject (e.g., 'the pen' represents the written press; 'the sword' represents military violence).

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Figurative Language, Tropes, and Rhetorical Devices
questions.Question: When a part of something is deliberately used to represent the whole, as in 'all hands on deck' or 'give us this day our daily bread', the figure is:
questions.OptionA: Metonymy
questions.OptionB: Synecdoche
questions.OptionC: Euphemism
questions.OptionD: Litotes
questions.Option_a: Metonymy
questions.Option_b: Synecdoche
questions.Option_c: Euphemism
questions.Option_d: Litotes
questions.Explanation: Synecdoche is a specific trope where a part stands for the whole (e.g. 'hands' for sailors/labourers) or the whole stands for a part.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Figurative Language, Tropes, and Rhetorical Devices
questions.Question: The direct rhetorical address to an absent or dead person, an abstract quality, or an inanimate entity as though it were alive and present is an:
questions.OptionA: Allusion
questions.OptionB: Eulogy
questions.OptionC: Apostrophe
questions.OptionD: Assonance
questions.Option_a: Allusion
questions.Option_b: Eulogy
questions.Option_c: Apostrophe
questions.Option_d: Assonance
questions.Explanation: An apostrophe is an exclamatory rhetorical figure where the speaker addresses an absent person or personified abstraction (e.g. 'O Death, where is thy sting?').

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Figurative Language, Tropes, and Rhetorical Devices
questions.Question: An understatement achieved by affirming something through the negation of its opposite, such as saying 'He is no fool' to mean he is very wise, is:
questions.OptionA: Zeugma
questions.OptionB: Hyperbole
questions.OptionC: Innuendo
questions.OptionD: Litotes
questions.Option_a: Zeugma
questions.Option_b: Hyperbole
questions.Option_c: Innuendo
questions.Option_d: Litotes
questions.Explanation: Litotes is ironical understatement where an affirmative sentiment is expressed by negating its contrary (e.g., 'not a bad performance').

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Figurative Language, Tropes, and Rhetorical Devices
questions.Question: Dramatic Irony occurs when:
questions.OptionA: The audience or reader possesses vital knowledge that a character on stage is unaware of, creating suspense and deeper significance in their words
questions.OptionB: A character intentionally utters sarcastic insults to hurt an opponent
questions.OptionC: An unexpected thunderstorm occurs precisely during an outdoor wedding
questions.OptionD: The ending of a story is completely omitted by the author
questions.Option_a: The audience or reader possesses vital knowledge that a character on stage is unaware of, creating suspense and deeper significance in their words
questions.Option_b: A character intentionally utters sarcastic insults to hurt an opponent
questions.Option_c: An unexpected thunderstorm occurs precisely during an outdoor wedding
questions.Option_d: The ending of a story is completely omitted by the author
questions.Explanation: Dramatic irony arises when the audience understands the true reality or future catastrophe while the character acts in tragic ignorance of it.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Figurative Language, Tropes, and Rhetorical Devices
questions.Question: The substitution of a mild, gentle, or indirect expression for one that is harsh, unpleasant, or socially taboo (such as 'passed away' for died) is a(n):
questions.OptionA: Epigram
questions.OptionB: Euphemism
questions.OptionC: Epitaph
questions.OptionD: Malapropism
questions.Option_a: Epigram
questions.Option_b: Euphemism
questions.Option_c: Epitaph
questions.Option_d: Malapropism
questions.Explanation: A euphemism replaces blunt or distressing language with a softer, polite phrase (e.g., 'pass away', 'let go' instead of fired).

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Figurative Language, Tropes, and Rhetorical Devices
questions.Question: What figure of speech is present in: 'The politician was generous with other people's money'?
questions.OptionA: Onomatopoeia
questions.OptionB: Simile
questions.OptionC: Irony / Innuendo
questions.OptionD: Anaphora
questions.Option_a: Onomatopoeia
questions.Option_b: Simile
questions.Option_c: Irony / Innuendo
questions.Option_d: Anaphora
questions.Explanation: This uses irony and innuendo to satirize the politician's pretense of generosity while actually spending public funds.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Figurative Language, Tropes, and Rhetorical Devices
questions.Question: A humorous play on words that sound identical or similar but carry completely different meanings is a:
questions.OptionA: Solecism
questions.OptionB: Cliché
questions.OptionC: Parody
questions.OptionD: Pun (Paronomasia)
questions.Option_a: Solecism
questions.Option_b: Cliché
questions.Option_c: Parody
questions.Option_d: Pun (Paronomasia)
questions.Explanation: A pun exploits multiple meanings of a word or similar-sounding words for humorous or rhetorical effect.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Poetic Forms, Meter, Rhyme, and Rhythm
questions.Question: How is a traditional Italian (Petrarchan) Sonnet structurally organized?
questions.OptionA: An octave (eight lines) rhyming abbaabba followed by a sestet (six lines) rhyming cdecde or cdcdcd
questions.OptionB: Three quatrains rhyming abab cdcd efef followed by a rhyming couplet gg
questions.OptionC: Seven unrhymed couplets composed in dactylic hexameter
questions.OptionD: Two stanzas of seven lines each rhyming aabbccd
questions.Option_a: An octave (eight lines) rhyming abbaabba followed by a sestet (six lines) rhyming cdecde or cdcdcd
questions.Option_b: Three quatrains rhyming abab cdcd efef followed by a rhyming couplet gg
questions.Option_c: Seven unrhymed couplets composed in dactylic hexameter
questions.Option_d: Two stanzas of seven lines each rhyming aabbccd
questions.Explanation: The Petrarchan sonnet consists of an octave that presents a problem or situation, and a sestet that resolves it, separated by a volta (turn).

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Poetic Forms, Meter, Rhyme, and Rhythm
questions.Question: The English (Shakespearean) Sonnet concludes with which distinctive structural unit?
questions.OptionA: An unrhymed triplet in trochaic meter
questions.OptionB: A rhyming heroic couplet (gg) that summarizes or reverses the preceding three quatrains
questions.OptionC: A four-line refrain repeated from the opening stanza
questions.OptionD: A prose postscript explaining the speaker's emotional state
questions.Option_a: An unrhymed triplet in trochaic meter
questions.Option_b: A rhyming heroic couplet (gg) that summarizes or reverses the preceding three quatrains
questions.Option_c: A four-line refrain repeated from the opening stanza
questions.Option_d: A prose postscript explaining the speaker's emotional state
questions.Explanation: A Shakespearean sonnet comprises three quatrains (abab cdcd efef) followed by a final rhyming couplet (gg) delivering an epigrammatic conclusion.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Poetic Forms, Meter, Rhyme, and Rhythm
questions.Question: The dramatic shift in tone, thought, or emotional perspective occurring between the octave and sestet in a sonnet is known as the:
questions.OptionA: Enjambment
questions.OptionB: Caesura
questions.OptionC: Volta (turn)
questions.OptionD: Refrain
questions.Option_a: Enjambment
questions.Option_b: Caesura
questions.Option_c: Volta (turn)
questions.Option_d: Refrain
questions.Explanation: The volta is the dramatic turn or pivot in thought and argument in a sonnet, typically occurring at line 9.

questions.Subject: Literature
questions.Topic: Poetic Forms, Meter, Rhyme, and Rhythm
questions.Question: Blank Verse is defined in English poetry as verse that consists of:
questions.OptionA: Short humorous stanzas of five lines rhyming aabba
questions.OptionB: Rhymed lines without any metrical rhythm or structure
questions.OptionC: Poetry composed without punctuation or capital letters
questions.OptionD: Unrhymed lines of iambic pentameter
questions.Option_a: Short humorous stanzas of five lines rhyming aabba
questions.Option_b: Rhymed lines without any metrical rhythm or structure
questions.Option_c: Poetry composed without punctuation or capital letters
